extracted.intended_audience: readers of political philosophy, students, policymakers, and the educated public interested in civil liberty
extracted.subtask_description: A canonical statement of the limits of societal and governmental interference with individual action (Mill's harm principle) and related liberties: thought, expression, tastes, pursuits, and association, with exceptions for immaturity and special cases. The text explains when interference is justified and gives examples and caveats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm Principle / self-protection as sole justification for interference
rubrics_metrics.description: The sole end for which mankind are warranted, individually or collectively, in interfering with the liberty of action of any of their number, is self-protection. The only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilized community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: His own good, physical or moral, is not a sufficient warrant for compulsion; reasons such as that an act would make him happier or wiser justify remonstration, persuasion, or entreaty, but not compulsion. To justify compulsion, the conduct must be calculated to produce evil to some one else.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability only to mature persons
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine applies only to human beings in the maturity of their faculties; not to children, young persons below the legal age of manhood or womanhood, or to societies in an immature ('barbarian') state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who require care must be protected against their own actions; despotism may be legitimate in dealing with 'barbarians' if the end is their improvement and the means actually effect that end. Law may fix ages for responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between self-regarding and other-regarding conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Only that part of an individual's conduct which concerns others is amenable to society's control; in the part which merely concerns himself, his independence is, of right, absolute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Society may hold a person responsible for actions that harm others; when conduct affects others only with their free, voluntary, and undeceived consent, society has only an indirect interest. The inward domain of consciousness is excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of thought, conscience, and expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty of conscience, thought, and feeling: absolute freedom of opinion and sentiment on all subjects (practical, speculative, scientific, moral, or theological). Expressing and publishing opinions is practically inseparable from liberty of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protection is required against both legal penalties and the moral coercion of public opinion. Freedom of expression is of great importance and rests largely on the same reasons as freedom of thought itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of tastes and pursuits (individuality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty to frame the plan of one's life to suit one's own character: freedom of tastes and pursuits; doing as one likes so long as it does not harm others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals should be free to live as they choose even if others think the conduct foolish, perverse, or wrong; the proper guardian of one's health (bodily, mental, spiritual) is the individual himself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of combination / association
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom to unite (combine) with others for any purpose not involving harm to others, provided the persons combining are of full age and not forced or deceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows from individual liberty and is part of the appropriate region of human liberty; combinations that involve harm to others fall outside this liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal compulsion justified for preventing harm to others and for certain positive duties
rubrics_metrics.description: If one does an act hurtful to others, that is prima facie a case for punishment by law or general disapprobation; there are also positive acts for the benefit of others which one may rightfully be compelled to perform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of compellable positive acts: to give evidence in court, to bear one's fair share in the common defence, to perform duties like saving a fellow-creature's life. Compulsion for omission (inaction) requires more cautious exercise than for action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between punishment by law and social disapprobation
rubrics_metrics.description: Society can respond to harmful conduct either through legal penalties or by general disapprobation; legal penalties are appropriate where they can be safely applied, else disapprobation may be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral coercion by public opinion can be more penetrating than legal sanctions and requires protection against misuse; choices about which instrument to use depend on the safety and appropriateness of legal penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility for actions versus omissions
rubrics_metrics.description: A person may cause evil to others by action or by inaction and is accountable in either case; however, holding someone responsible for not preventing evil (omission) is an exception requiring stronger justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inaction cases justify compulsion only in clear and grave instances; reasons for not enforcing responsibility include that the agent likely acts better when left to discretion or that control would produce greater evils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection against the tyranny of the majority and social opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Society collectively can be a tyrant over individuals through prevailing opinion and feeling as well as through political acts; protection is required against such social tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social mandates can penetrate the details of life and 'enslave the soul'; limits on collective opinion's interference are as necessary as limits on political despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility as the ultimate appeal (but in a broad sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author foregoes appeals to abstract right and regards utility as the ultimate appeal on ethical questions, but utility in the largest sense grounded on the permanent interests of a man as a progressive being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conception of utility justifies subjecting individual spontaneity to external control only with respect to actions concerning the interests of others; human development in its richest diversity is the grand principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits where interference would cause greater evils or where individual discretion is preferable
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when others are concerned, there are cases where reasons of expediency or likely outcomes preclude enforcement of responsibility: either because the agent is likely to act better if left alone, or because attempting control would produce greater evils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When such reasons preclude enforcement, the agent's conscience should act to protect others' interests in the absence of external compulsion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate region of human liberty (inward domain)
rubrics_metrics.description: The appropriate region of human liberty comprises the inward domain of consciousness (liberty of conscience, thought, feeling), liberty of tastes and pursuits, and liberty of combination within the same limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whatever affects oneself directly is in this region; whatever affects others may fall outside unless consent and participation are free, voluntary, and undeceived.

rubrics_metrics.name: The only freedom deserving the name
rubrics_metrics.description: The only freedom which deserves the name is that of pursuing our own good in our own way, so long as we do not attempt to deprive others of theirs, or impede their efforts to obtain it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mankind benefit more by suffering each other to live as they see fit than by compelling uniformity; complete and unqualified respect for the listed liberties is necessary for a society to be truly free.
